subject: english-literature
title: Free Indirect Discourse
welcome_lead: The shimmer between character and narrator — free indirect discourse is the workhorse of modern fiction.
meta_desc: Free indirect discourse, focalisation and narrative distance at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now spot the shimmer — that hovering between narrator's syntax and character's voice that defines modern prose.

concepts.def: Third-person narration that adopts a character's idiom and viewpoint without quotation marks ('She wondered. Was it really Tuesday again?').
Genette's term — the perspective through which events are presented; internal, external or zero.
Reported speech with quotation marks: 'She said, "I am tired."'
Reported speech without quotation marks: 'She said she was tired.'
The perceived closeness between narrator and character, modulated by FID and focalisation.
French term for FID, especially associated with Flaubert's Madame Bovary.

walkthroughs.body_html:
FID lets a third-person narrator carry a character's idiom. She had to leave. Oh, why was Tuesday always so awful? — the question is hers, the syntax shared.

Austen perfected the technique; Flaubert turned it into a method; Joyce and Woolf radicalised it.

Genette distinguished zero focalisation (omniscient), internal focalisation (filtered through one character) and external focalisation (camera-like, no interiority).

The same event in different focalisations becomes radically different prose.

FID allows simultaneous identification and ironic distance. Austen lets us inhabit Emma's misjudgements while subtly noting them.

The technique is the engine of moral complexity in the novel.
